claim: γ-TuRC is a 2.2 megadalton, ring-shaped complex formed by γ-tubulin with γ-tubulin complex proteins (GCPs).
source: The universal nucleator, γ-tubulin efficiently nucleates MTs in vivo (Oakley and Oakley, 1989; Hannak et al., 2002; Groen et al., 2009) by forming a 2.2 megadalton, ring-shaped complex with γ-tubulin complex proteins (GCPs), known as the γ-Tubulin Ring Complex (γ-TuRC) (Moritz et al., 1995; Moritz et al., 1998; Zheng et al., 1995; Kollman et al., 2010; Kollman et al., 2015; Oegema et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior structural and biochemical studies of γ-TuRC.

claim: γ-TuRC positions a lateral array of 13 γ-tubulin molecules that template MT assembly by binding αβ-tubulin dimers and promoting their lateral interaction.
source: Structural studies (Kollman et al., 2010; Moritz et al., 2000; Liu et al., 2020; Wieczorek et al., 2020; Consolati et al., 2020) have revealed that γ-TuRC positions a lateral array of 13 γ-tubulin molecules that are thought to template MT assembly by binding αβ-tubulin dimers and promoting their lateral interaction to result in nucleation of a MT (Kollman et al., 2010; Moritz et al., 2000; Keating and Borisy, 2000; Wiese and Zheng, 2000; Kollman et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies and the widely accepted model of γ-TuRC function.

claim: MT nucleation from γ-TuRC molecules has not been directly visualized in real time prior to this study.
source: Despite this model being widely accepted, MT nucleation from γ-TuRC molecules has not been directly visualized in real time and the dynamics of nucleation of a MT from αβ-tubulin dimers remains to be characterized.
evidence: Statement about the state of the field prior to this work.

claim: Single, attached γ-TuRC molecules assemble αβ-tubulin into a MT de novo starting from zero length.
source: Kymographs revealed that single, attached γ-TuRC molecules assembled αβ-tubulin into a MT de novo starting from zero length within the diffraction limit of light microscopy (Figure 1C), ruling out an alternative model where MTs first spontaneously nucleate and then become stabilized via γ-TuRC.
evidence: Directly observed in kymographs shown in Figure 1C from single molecule microscopy experiments.

claim: γ-TuRC caps the MT minus-end while only the plus-end polymerizes.
source: By observing fiduciary marks on the MT lattice (Figure 1C) and generating polarity-marked MTs from attached γ-TuRC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), we show that γ-TuRC caps the MT minus-end while only the plus-end polymerizes, as supported by previous works (Keating and Borisy, 2000; Wiese and Zheng, 2000).
evidence: Observed experimentally through fiduciary marks and polarity-marked MTs, supported by prior citations.

claim: γ-TuRC persists on the MT minus-end for the duration of the experiments without detachment.
source: Notably, the detachment of γ-TuRC molecules and re-growth of the MT minus-ends were not observed, and γ-TuRC persists on the MT minus-end for the duration of our experiments.
evidence: Direct observation from time-lapse experiments.

claim: γ-TuRC nucleates MTs starting from 7 μM tubulin concentration.
source: γ-TuRCs nucleated MTs starting from 7 μM tubulin (Figure 2A–B), which is higher than the minimum tubulin concentration (C*) needed for growth from a pre-formed MT plus-end (C*=1.4 μM, Figure 2B).
evidence: Measured experimentally by titrating tubulin concentration, shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The critical concentration for MT polymerization from pre-formed MT plus-ends is 1.4 μM.
source: γ-TuRCs nucleated MTs starting from 7 μM tubulin (Figure 2A–B), which is higher than the minimum tubulin concentration (C*) needed for growth from a pre-formed MT plus-end (C*=1.4 μM, Figure 2B).
evidence: Determined from linear fit of growth speed versus tubulin concentration in Figure 2B.

claim: The number of MTs nucleated from γ-TuRC increases non-linearly with αβ-tubulin concentration.
source: Furthermore, the number of MTs nucleated from γ-TuRC increased non-linearly with αβ-tubulin concentration as opposed to the linear increase in MT's growth speed with tubulin concentration (Figure 2B).
evidence: Observed experimentally and shown in Figure 2B inset.

claim: The cooperative assembly of 3.9 ± 0.5 αβ-tubulin subunits on γ-TuRC represents the rate-limiting step in MT nucleation.
source: The power-law dependence on αβ-tubulin concentration (Figure 2D) yields the number of tubulin dimers, 3.9 ± 0.5, that compose the rate-limiting, transition state during MT assembly from γ-TuRC (Figure 2D).
evidence: Calculated from power-law analysis of nucleation rate versus tubulin concentration, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Spontaneous MT nucleation requires a higher concentration of 14 μM tubulin.
source: In contrast to γ-TuRC-mediated nucleation, a higher concentration of 14 μM tubulin was required for any spontaneous assembly of MTs, after which both the plus- and minus-ends polymerize (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Video 4).
evidence: Measured experimentally in spontaneous nucleation assays, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Spontaneous MT nucleation requires cooperative assembly of 8.1 ± 0.9 αβ-tubulin dimers in the rate-limiting intermediate.
source: The number of MTs assembled as a function of the αβ-tubulin concentration displayed a power-law dependence with an even larger exponent of 8.1 ± 0.9 (Figure 3C), indicating a highly cooperative process that requires 8 αβ-tubulin dimers in a rate-limiting intermediate, in agreement with previous reports (Voter and Erickson, 1984; Flyvbjerg et al., 1996).
evidence: Calculated from power-law analysis of spontaneous nucleation data, shown in Figure 3C, and agrees with prior literature.

claim: γ-TuRC nucleates MTs significantly more efficiently than spontaneous MT assembly.
source: Further, direct comparison and measurement of spontaneous MT assembly with γ-TuRC-mediated nucleation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C) clearly demonstrates that γ-TuRC nucleates MTs significantly more efficiently.
evidence: Direct experimental comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: MT assembly from blunt seeds occurs with a cooperativity of 1 ± 0.3 αβ-tubulin dimers.
source: The measured reaction kinetics as a function of the αβ-tubulin concentration (Figure 3D) was used to obtain the power-law of the nucleation rate, 1 ± 0.3 (Figure 3E).
evidence: Calculated from power-law analysis of MT assembly from blunt seeds, shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Addition of a single αβ-tubulin dimer is sufficient to overcome the rate-limiting barrier for MT assembly from blunt seeds.
source: This suggests that in our assay condition, blunt MT ends assemble tubulin dimers into the MT lattice non-cooperatively. In other words, the addition of a single αβ-tubulin dimer suffices to overcome the rate-limiting barrier, which also occurs during the polymerization phase of MT dynamics.
evidence: Inferred from the cooperativity of ~1 measured for blunt seed assembly.

claim: γ-tubulin binds to αβ-tubulin at both 10 μM and 35 μM αβ-tubulin concentrations as shown by size-exclusion chromatography.
source: Interestingly, in the presence of either 10 μM (low) or 35 μM (high) concentrations of αβ-tubulin, the γ-tubulin binds to αβ-tubulin (pseudo-colored profile in cyan) and elutes earlier, specifically in fraction H (Figure 4A (ii-iii), yellow arrow).
evidence: Observed in size-exclusion chromatography experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The heterogeneous γ-/αβ-tubulin affinity is higher than the αβ-/αβ-tubulin affinity.
source: This suggests that the heterogeneous γ-/αβ-tubulin affinity is higher than the αβ-/αβ-tubulin affinity.
evidence: Inferred from size-exclusion chromatography showing γ-tubulin binds αβ-tubulin at lower concentrations than αβ-tubulin self-association.

claim: 15-fold more γ-tubulin molecules bind to surface-attached αβ-tubulin than αβ-tubulin molecules in single molecule microscopy assays.
source: While both fluorescent αβ-tubulin and γ-tubulin specifically bind to surface-attached αβ-tubulin, 15-fold more γ-tubulin molecules were bound than αβ-tubulin molecules (Figure 4C), further supporting a stronger γ-/αβ-tubulin interaction.
evidence: Measured by single molecule microscopy and quantified in Figure 4C.

claim: Purified γ-tubulin at high concentrations efficiently nucleates MTs from αβ-tubulin subunits and caps MT minus-ends.
source: In performing the above experiments, we unexpectedly found that purified γ-tubulin on its own, at high concentrations and at 33°C, efficiently nucleated MTs from αβ-tubulin subunits (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) and capped MT minus-ends while allowing plus-ends to polymerize (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Observed experimentally in nucleation assays with purified γ-tubulin, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: γ-tubulin at high concentrations forms filaments in vitro of variable widths.
source: Besides its ability to form higher order oligomers in a physiological buffer (Thawani et al., 2018), γ-tubulin at high concentrations also forms filaments in vitro of variable widths (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C; Moritz and Agard, unpublished results) as assayed by negative stain electron microscopy (EM).
evidence: Observed by negative stain EM shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, supported by prior work and unpublished results.

claim: γ-tubulins self-assemble into lateral arrays with a repeating unit of approximately 54 Å.
source: To understand the nature of these filaments, we generated 3D reconstructions, which revealed that γ-tubulins self-assemble into lateral arrays with a repeating unit of approximately 54 Å (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–E).
evidence: Determined from 3D reconstructions of γ-tubulin filaments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D-E.

claim: The 54 Å repeat in γ-tubulin filaments closely matches the lateral tubulin repeats in the MT lattice and γ-tubulin crystal contacts, but not the longitudinal αβ-tubulin repeat.
source: This closely matches the lateral tubulin repeats in the MT lattice (PDB:6DPU [Zhang et al., 2018; Zhang and Nogales, 2018]) and in γ-tubulin crystal contacts (52 Å, PDB:1Z5W [Aldaz et al., 2005a; Aldaz et al., 2005b]), but not the longitudinal αβ-tubulin repeat (40 Å).
evidence: Comparison with known structural data from PDB entries.

claim: Laterally associated γ-tubulin are sufficient to efficiently nucleate MTs.
source: This suggests that laterally associated γ-tubulin are sufficient to efficiently nucleate MTs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that γ-tubulin forms lateral arrays and nucleates MTs efficiently.

claim: Monte Carlo simulations recapitulate the dynamics of MT nucleation from γ-TuRC.
source: The resulting model produces a sharp transition from zero-MT length to a continuously growing MT upon γ-TuRC closure (Figure 5B) that occurs at variable time points for each realization of the model (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C(i)). This qualitatively recapitulates the dynamics of γ-TuRC-mediated nucleation events observed experimentally.
evidence: Simulations shown in Figure 5B match experimental observations.

claim: The most probable transition state is composed of four αβ-tubulin arranged on neighboring sites that form three lateral bonds when γ-TuRC transitions to a closed conformation.
source: The most probable transition state is composed of four αβ-tubulin arranged on neighboring sites that form three lateral bonds when the γ-TuRC conformation changes to a closed one.
evidence: Determined from analysis of transition states in simulations, shown in Figure 5D.

claim: CDK5RAP2's γ-TuNA domain increases γ-TuRC-mediated nucleation only by 1.4-fold.
source: Measurement of nucleation activity revealed that CDK5RAP2's γ-TuNA domain increases γ-TuRC-mediated nucleation only by 1.4 (±0.02) -fold (mean ± std, n = 2) at t = 180 s, falling within the 95% confidence intervals of the control reactions (Figure 6A–B and Video 6).
evidence: Measured experimentally in nucleation assays with γ-TuNA, shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: NME7 does not increase γ-TuRC's nucleation activity when added at saturating concentrations.
source: Another putative activator, NME7 (Liu et al., 2014), when added to γ-TuRC at saturating concentrations (Wühr et al., 2014; Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Video 6), did not increase γ-TuRC's nucleation activity (Figure 6B).
evidence: Measured experimentally in nucleation assays with NME7, shown in Figure 6B.

claim: TPX2 has a small increase on the nucleation activity of γ-TuRC by 1.2-fold.
source: TPX2 also had a small increase on the nucleation activity of γ-TuRC by 1.2 (±0.3) -fold (mean ± std, n = 3) at t = 180 s, but bound strongly along the MT lattice (Figure 6C–D and Video 6).
evidence: Measured experimentally in nucleation assays with TPX2, shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: XMAP215 induces many surface-attached γ-TuRCs to nucleate MTs at low tubulin concentrations, resulting in a 25-fold increase in number of nucleated MTs.
source: Strikingly, the addition of XMAP215 induced many surface-attached γ-TuRCs to nucleate MTs, resulting in a drastic increase in number of nucleated MTs by 25 (±9) -fold (mean ±std, n = 3) within t = 120 s (Figure 7A–B, Fig. Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and Video 7).
evidence: Measured experimentally in nucleation assays with XMAP215, shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: XMAP215 and γ-TuRC molecules form a complex before MT nucleation occurs.
source: By directly visualizing γ-TuRC and XMAP215 molecules during the nucleation reaction (Figure 7C), we found that XMAP215 and γ-TuRC molecules first form a complex from which a MT was then nucleated (Figure 7C and Video 8).
evidence: Directly observed in triple-color fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 7C.

claim: For 76% of nucleation events, XMAP215 persists on γ-TuRC for three to ≥300 seconds before MT nucleation.
source: For 76% of the events (n = 56), XMAP215 visibly persisted between three to ≥300 s on γ-TuRC before MT nucleation.
evidence: Quantified from direct observation of XMAP215 binding to γ-TuRC in time-lapse experiments.

claim: XMAP215 effectively decreases the minimal tubulin concentration necessary for MT nucleation from γ-TuRC to 1.6 μM.
source: XMAP215 effectively decreases the minimal tubulin concentration necessary for MT nucleation from γ-TuRC to 1.6 μM (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), very close to the minimal concentration for plus-end polymerization.
evidence: Measured experimentally by titrating tubulin with XMAP215 present, shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cooperative nucleation by XMAP215 and γ-TuRC requires 3.3 ± 0.8 αβ-tubulin dimers in the transition state.
source: As before, we calculated the composition of the transition state by measuring the power-law dependence between the MT nucleation rate and tubulin concentration with a resulting cooperative assembly of 3.3 ± 0.8 αβ-tubulin dimers occurs (Figure 7E).
evidence: Calculated from power-law analysis of nucleation kinetics with XMAP215, shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Neither the N-terminus nor the C-terminus of XMAP215 alone stimulate additional nucleation from γ-TuRC.
source: Further, neither the N-terminus, containing TOG1-4 domains, nor the C-terminus of XMAP215, containing the TOG5 and C-terminal domain that directly interact with γ-tubulin (Thawani et al., 2018), stimulate additional nucleation from γ-TuRC (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Measured experimentally with XMAP215 truncations, shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Simulations where both longitudinal γ-/αβ-tubulin and αβ-/αβ-tubulin bond energies are increased by 1.2-fold capture the accelerated kinetics of MT nucleation by XMAP215.
source: Instead, simulations where both the longitudinal γ-/αβ-tubulin and αβ-/αβ-tubulin bond energies are increased by 1.2-fold captures the accelerated kinetics of MT nucleation at low αβ-tubulin concentrations.
evidence: Computational simulations shown in Figure 7D-E match experimental data when both bond energies are increased.

claim: XMAP215 strengthens the longitudinal γ-/αβ-tubulin bond to function as a nucleation factor.
source: Most importantly, our results show that, while the transition state is defined by γ-TuRC's conformation, XMAP215 strengthens the longitudinal γ-/αβ-tubulin bond to function as a bona-fide nucleation factor.
evidence: Inferred from simulations and experimental data showing XMAP215 enhances nucleation without changing cooperativity.

claim: Sub-endogenous concentration of MCAK is sufficient to nearly abolish MT nucleation from γ-TuRC molecules.
source: We find that addition of either sub-endogenous concentration of MCAK, or near-endogenous Stathmin concentration (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and Video 9) was sufficient to nearly abolish MT nucleation from all γ-TuRC molecules.
evidence: Measured experimentally in nucleation assays with MCAK, shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Near-endogenous Stathmin concentration is sufficient to nearly abolish MT nucleation from γ-TuRC molecules.
source: We find that addition of either sub-endogenous concentration of MCAK, or near-endogenous Stathmin concentration (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and Video 9) was sufficient to nearly abolish MT nucleation from all γ-TuRC molecules.
evidence: Measured experimentally in nucleation assays with Stathmin, shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Native γ-TuRC structure shows an open conformation where adjacent γ-tubulin do not form lateral interactions.
source: Moreover, the structure of native γ-TuRC shows an open conformation where adjacent γ-tubulin do not form a lateral interaction (Liu et al., 2020; Wieczorek et al., 2020; Consolati et al., 2020), raising further questions on how the conformational mismatch impacts γ-TuRC's nucleation activity (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by recent cryo-EM structures cited.

claim: γ-TuRC may transition to a closed conformation during MT assembly to match the geometry of αβ-tubulin dimers arranged laterally in the MT lattice.
source: It has been widely proposed that γ-TuRC may transition to a closed conformation during MT assembly to match the geometry of αβ-tubulin dimers arranged laterally in the MT lattice (Kollman et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: Widely proposed model supported by citations.

claim: At 10-15% of γ-TuRCs nucleate MTs at the highest tubulin concentrations tested in TIRF assays.
source: At the highest tubulin concentrations tested, approximately 10–15% of γ-TuRCs nucleate MTs in the TIRF assays (see Materials and Methods).
evidence: Calculated from experiments with labeled γ-TuRC as described in Materials and Methods.

claim: γ-TuRC-mediated nucleation has distinct characteristics from MT polymerization and assembly from blunt MT seeds.
source: Here, we show several lines of evidence that γ-TuRC-mediated nucleation has distinct characteristics from MT polymerization and assembly from blunt MT seeds.
evidence: Summary statement supported by multiple experimental comparisons in the manuscript.

claim: γ-TuRC molecules do not nucleate MTs at low tubulin concentration where MT polymerization can occur.
source: While growth speed of MTs nucleated from γ-TuRC or templated from MT seeds is similar (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), γ-TuRC molecules do not nucleate MTs at low tubulin concentration where MT polymerization can occur.
evidence: Observed experimentally by comparing nucleation from γ-TuRC versus seeds at different tubulin concentrations.

claim: Increasing tubulin concentration results in a non-linear increase in the number of γ-TuRCs molecules that nucleate MT, as opposed to a linear increase in rate of assembly from seeds.
source: Further increasing tubulin concentration results in a non-linear increase in the number of γ-TuRCs molecules that nucleate MT, as opposed to a linear increase in rate of assembly from seeds.
evidence: Observed experimentally in concentration titration experiments.

claim: The rate-limiting transition state on γ-TuRC is composed of four αβ-tubulin dimers in contrast with MT polymerization where one tubulin dimer suffices.
source: In summary, the rate-limiting transition state on γ-TuRC is composed of four αβ-tubulin dimers in contrast with MT polymerization where one tubulin dimer suffices to overcome the slowest step.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings comparing cooperativity of γ-TuRC nucleation versus seed assembly.

claim: The high affinity of γ-/αβ-tubulin interaction increases the dwell time of αβ-tubulin dimers on γ-TuRC and promotes γ-TuRC's MT nucleation activity.
source: Instead, our biochemical investigation show that the high affinity of γ-/αβ-tubulin interaction increases the dwell time of αβ-tubulin dimers on γ-TuRC and promotes γ-TuRC's MT nucleation activity, as predicted by our modeling.
evidence: Supported by biochemical measurements and computational modeling.

claim: The open γ-TuRC conformation and its transition to a closed one defines γ-TuRC's nucleation activity and transition state.
source: In sum, building on the recent structural work (Liu et al., 2020; Wieczorek et al., 2020; Consolati et al., 2020), our results show that the open γ-TuRC conformation and its transition to a closed one defines γ-TuRC's nucleation activity and transition state.
evidence: Summary conclusion integrating structural data with experimental and computational findings.

claim: Locally concentrating soluble αβ-tubulin could upregulate the levels of γ-TuRC-mediated MT nucleation.
source: In this model, locally concentrating soluble αβ-tubulin could upregulate the levels of γ-TuRC-mediated MT nucleation, for example as recently shown through accumulation of high concentration of tubulin dimers at the centrosome by MAPs (Woodruff et al., 2017; Baumgart et al., 2019) and by co-condensation of tubulin on MTs by TPX2 during branching MT nucleation (King and Petry, 2020), and finally via specific recruitment of tubulin on γ-TuRC through the binding of XMAP215 as shown here (Thawani et al., 2018; Gunzelmann et al., 2018; Flor-Parra et al., 2018).
evidence: Proposed mechanism supported by recent literature and findings from this study.

claim: XMAP215 functions synergistically with γ-TuRC.
source: Altogether, our results confirm that XMAP215 indeed functions synergistically with γ-TuRC, in agreement with recent works (Consolati et al., 2020; Thawani et al., 2018; Gunzelmann et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and agreement with recent literature.

claim: γ-TuRC-mediated nucleation is inhibited by MAPs that inhibit MT polymerization.
source: Thus, γ-TuRC-mediated nucleation is inhibited by MAPs that inhibit MT polymerization.
evidence: Observed experimentally with MCAK and Stathmin.

claim: In spontaneous nucleation, both the plus- and minus-ends of assembled MTs polymerize.
source: In contrast to γ-TuRC-mediated nucleation, a higher concentration of 14 μM tubulin was required for any spontaneous assembly of MTs, after which both the plus- and minus-ends polymerize (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Video 4).
evidence: Observed in kymographs of spontaneously nucleated MTs shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Specific attachment of γ-TuRC to coverslips is required to observe the nucleation activity.
source: Notably, specific attachment of γ-TuRC to coverslips is also required to observe the nucleation activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by control experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: For 50% of nucleation events with XMAP215, some XMAP215 molecules remained on the minus-end together with γ-TuRC after MT nucleation.
source: For 50% of nucleation events (n = 58), some XMAP215 molecules remained on the minus-end together with γ-TuRC, while for the other 50% of events, XMAP215 was not observed on the minus-end after nucleation.
evidence: Quantified from direct observation in triple-color fluorescence microscopy experiments.

claim: XMAP215 molecules nucleate with γ-TuRC and then continue polymerization of the plus-end.
source: This suggests that XMAP215 molecules nucleate with γ-TuRC and then continue polymerization of the plus-end.
evidence: Inferred from observation that XMAP215 tracks with the MT plus-end after nucleation.

claim: The contribution of the blunt-end geometry of γ-TuRC in defining the kinetics of nucleation and its transition state is minimal.
source: To conclude, while the γ-TuRC positions a blunt plus-end of γ-tubulins, the contribution of this specific end architecture in defining the kinetics of nucleation from γ-TuRC and its transition state is minimal.
evidence: Concluded from comparison of nucleation kinetics between γ-TuRC and blunt seeds.

claim: Prior to MT nucleation, longitudinal association of individual αβ-tubulins to γ-tubulin sites on open γ-TuRC occurs, and these αβ-tubulins dissociate rapidly in the absence of lateral bond energy.
source: First, prior to MT nucleation, we observe longitudinal association of individual αβ-tubulins either to the γ-tubulin sites on the open γ-TuRC or, less frequently, with existing αβ-tubulin in a protofilament (Figure 5B, left insets). These αβ-tubulins dissociate rapidly in the absence of additional lateral bond energy.
evidence: Observed in simulation time traces shown in Figure 5B.

claim: At the transition state, many αβ-tubulin dimers stochastically assemble on neighboring sites on γ-TuRC, and favorable Gibbs free energy from lateral interactions overcomes the energy penalty of conformational change.
source: At the sharp transition prior to MT assembly (Figure 5B, right insets), we find that many αβ-tubulin dimers stochastically assemble on neighboring sites on γ-TuRC. Favorable Gibbs free energy from the lateral interaction between these αβ-tubulin dimers overcomes the energy penalty of the conformational change and transitions γ-TuRC into a closed state.
evidence: Observed in simulation time traces and analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A variable total number of αβ-tubulin dimers with an average of 5.2 ± 1 are present on γ-TuRC at the transition state.
source: A variable total number of αβ-tubulin dimers with an average of 5.2 ± 1 (n = 2119 simulations) were present on γ-TuRC at the transition state (Figure 5D, left).
evidence: Calculated from analysis of 2119 simulations shown in Figure 5D.

claim: αβ-tubulin subunits in the transition state assemble on neighboring sites into laterally arranged groupings.
source: To our surprise, αβ-tubulin subunits in the transition state assemble on neighboring sites into laterally arranged groupings (Figure 5D, right).
evidence: Observed in 3D probability distribution of transition states shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In the transition states, the free energy gained from lateral bonds between αβ-tubulins compensates for the thermodynamic barrier posed by γ-TuRC's open conformation.
source: Most importantly, in these transition states, the free energy gained from the lateral bonds between αβ-tubulins compensates for the thermodynamic barrier posed by γ-TuRC's open conformation to allow for MT nucleation.
evidence: Inferred from simulation results and thermodynamic analysis.

claim: The laterally-arranged group of 4 αβ-tubulin dimers physically represents the power-law exponent measured from average nucleation kinetics.
source: Notably, the laterally-arranged group of 4 αβ-tubulin dimers physically represents the power-law exponent measured from the average nucleation kinetics (Figure 2D).
evidence: Connection between simulation results and experimental power-law analysis.

claim: Endogenous γ-TuRC was purified from Xenopus egg extracts.
source: To study how γ-TuRC nucleates a MT, we purified endogenous γ-TuRC from Xenopus egg extracts and biotinylated the complexes to immobilize them on functionalized glass (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Described in methods and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Major known γ-TuRC components were detected in the purified protein, and GCP2/3 are heavily biotinylated or Alexa-568 labeled during purification.
source: Major, known γ-TuRC components were detected in the purified protein and GCP2/3 are heavily biotinylated or Alexa-568 labeled during purification.
evidence: Shown in protein gel and immunoblot analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A 13-protofilament geometry for the MT lattice and γ-TuRC with a pitch of 3 tubulins was used in Monte Carlo simulations.
source: A 13-protofilament geometry for the MT lattice and γ-TuRC were used with a pitch of 3 tubulins (Figure 5A).
evidence: Described in simulation methods and shown in Figure 5A.
